A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Magnetic nanoparticles

α-Cyclodextrin β-Cyclodextrin γ-Cyclodextrin

Chronic kidney disease Adsorption

Uremic toxin Blood

A B S T R A C T

Chronic kidney disease entails a progressive decline in kidney function, hindering the kidneys’ ability to excrete fluid, electrolytes, and metabolites. This dysfunction leads to metabolite accumulation in the bloodstream, which can reach toxic concentrations. Hemodialysis is an effective means of treating patients with kidney failure, but it does not clear all toxins effectively. Engineered nano-adsorbents can potentially improve the removal of retained toxins, particularly protein-bound types. Magnetic nanoparticles coated with α-, β-, and γ-cyclodextrin were synthesized, and physicochemical properties were characterized using thermogravimetric analysis, transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, and ζ-potential for their physiochemical properties. The effect of surface chemistry and incubation time on toxin adsorption was investigated using quantitative mass spectrom-etry techniques. All particle types demonstrated toxin adsorption to some level. Overall, the adsorption process was independent of metabolite concentration, suggesting a dynamic interplay between surface properties and solution composition. This insight will contribute to developing innovative adsorbent films designed to remove uremic toxins effectively.

## Introduction

Kidney failure leads to the accumulation of metabolites in the blood. Although not all metabolites cause deleterious biological effects, me-tabolites that accumulate due to reduced kidney function are commonly referred to as ‘uremic toxins’ ([Webster, Nagler, Morton, & Masson,](#_bookmark53) [2017](#_bookmark53)). Hemodialysis (HD) is the primary treatment option for kidney failure, but morbidity and mortality for these patients remain unac-ceptably high ([Lawson, Niklason, & Roy-Chaudhury, 2020](#_bookmark27)). A reduced toxin clearance has been observed with a high total distribution volume ([Magnani & Atti, 2021](#_bookmark34); [Watanabe, Miyamoto, Otagiri, & Maruyama,](#_bookmark52) [2011](#_bookmark52)). In addition, uremic toxins that interact strongly with blood proteins (_i.e._, protein-bound uremic toxins, PBUTs) are also poorly removed by HD. Given these limitations in molecular clearance effi-ciencies, the lack of progress in advancing patient outcomes, and the projected rise of kidney disease to become the fifth leading cause of global mortality by 2040, a more efficient method for clearing toxins from the blood must be developed ([Vanholder et al., 2021](#_bookmark47)).

Adsorbent-based platforms have been proposed for removing uremic

toxins from the blood ([Gao, Zhang, Yang, Li, & Lin, 2022](#_bookmark20); [Ma, Li, Tonelli,](#_bookmark32) [& Unsworth, 2021](#_bookmark32)). Other than the apparent requirements for hemo-compatibility, an ideal adsorbent must have several properties, including the capacity to adsorb trace amounts of uremic toxins within a mixture of toxins, toxin specificity, and adsorbed stability of the bound toxin ([Li, Han, Xie, Liu, & Jia, 2020](#_bookmark29)). Nanoparticles possess noteworthy advantages, like high surface area and convective mass transfer prop-erties, that differentiate them significantly from other adsorbent forms in the context of blood toxin clearance. The capacity to engineer binding efficiencies through surface modification and their ability to target the removal of high molecular weight compounds has been shown and is an area where HD falls short ([Herrmann, Schlegel, Graf, Stark, & Beck-Schimmer, 2015](#_bookmark22)). A challenge to the application of nanoparticles to this problem is their retrieval; magnetic particles (MNP) are attractive as they can be extracted using an external magnetic field ([Herrmann et al.,](#_bookmark22) [2015](#_bookmark22)). Iron oxide particles, in particular, demonstrate promising po-tential for _in vivo_ application owing to their relative biocompatibility, straightforward functionalization process, low susceptibility for oxida-tion (_i.e._, Fe3O4 and γ-Fe2O3), and their benign biodegradation products

Cyclodextrins (CD) have been studied for binding small molecules, including some uremic toxins ([Li et al., 2018](#_bookmark28); [Li et al., 2023](#_bookmark31)). The high solubility of CDs, provided through exposed hydroxyl groups, coupled with the ability for host-guest complexation to occur _via_ the hydro-phobic cavity, make CDs promising for biomedical applications in gen-eral ([Crini, 2014](#_bookmark15); [Li et al., 2023](#_bookmark30); [Wang et al., 2022](#_bookmark50)). The increased number of D-glucose subunits found for native CDs influences the inner diameter of the hydrophobic cavity (α-CD; 4.7–5.3 Å, β-CD; 6.0–6.5 Å, γ-CD; 7.5–8.3 Å) ([Wankar et al., 2020](#_bookmark51); [Zhang, Liu, & Liu, 2020](#_bookmark57)). Spe-cifically, β-CD has been studied as an adsorbent for removing p-cresol sulfate, hippuric acid, and quinolinic acid from plasma ([Li et al., 2020](#_bookmark29)). Poly-β-CDs, when integrated with hemodialysis, demonstrated enhanced efficacy. By incorporating poly-CDs into the dialysate of the hemodialysis system as an adsorbent, they have been observed to facilitate the clearance of multiple uremic toxins: 96 % for p-cresol sulfate, 98 % for hippuric acid, and 97 % for quinolinic acid ([Li et al.,](#_bookmark29) [2020](#_bookmark29)). There remain several questions regarding the application of CDs as adsorbent coatings for magnetic particle applications, namely, their capacity to adsorb trace amounts of uremic toxins within a mixture of toxins, adsorption specificity, and the stability of adsorbed toxins, all of which have only recently started to be defined ([Li, Sharaf, Zhang, et al.,](#_bookmark31) [2023](#_bookmark31)). Our research group recently introduced a poly 2-(meth-acryloyloxy)ethyl phosphorylcholine-_co_\-β-CD-coated MNPs that showed promise as an effective adsorbent for adsorbing uremic toxins from so-lution ([Li, Sharaf, Zhang, et al., 2023](#_bookmark31)).

Building upon this, our hypothesis is that increasing the number of CDs present at the interface will increase the number of binding sites that improve the uremic toxin adsorption efficiency and stability from a complex mixture of uremic toxins. Moreover, our approach uses a less chemically intensive method for modifying the MNP surface to evaluate the adsorption dynamics of uremic toxins from a complex solution, quantifying the effects of film properties and incubation time on toxin adsorption ([Li, Sharaf, Zhang, et al., 2023](#_bookmark31)). This study is the first to explore the potential use of physisorbed CD-coated MNPs for under-standing what toxins bind and their bound stability from a complex

toxin system. To this end, physisorbed CD-coated iron oxide MNPs ([Falconi et al., 2021](#_bookmark19); [Hamza, Metzinger, & Metzinger-Le Meuth, 2020](#_bookmark21)) were prepared using the co-precipitation method ([Yallapu et al., 2011](#_bookmark55)) with all three native CDs (α-, β-, and γ-CD). A model solution of twenty-six uremic toxins, reflecting the physiological concentration of metab-olites found in the blood of CKD patients ([Table 1](#_bookmark3)), was used to evaluate the effects of MNP surface chemistry on metabolite adsorption amounts, stability, and specificity. CD-MNP particle size and surface film prop-erties were evaluated using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), trans-mission electron microscopy (TEM), dynamic light scattering (DLS), and ζ-potential measurements. The adsorption of uremic toxins was inves-tigated as a function of surface chemistry and incubation time using quantitative liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). In this systematic study, the chemical and physical properties of the CD-modified MNPs were comprehensively assessed. Elucidation of the dy-namic adsorption profile of uremic toxins from a model multi-toxin so-lution is critical to justify further studying these systems in more complex solutions like whole blood.

Ammonium hydroxide solution (25 %, Sigma Aldrich), and Sodium Citrate (Fisher Scientific).

Chemicals for experiments and LC-MS: Optima™ LC-MS grade methanol, formic acid, and water were purchased from Fisher Scientific. Nitrogen gas (99.9 %) was used in required chemical reactions. LC-MS grade ethanol, LC-MS grade acetonitrile, pure reference standard com-pounds, and Nunc® 96 DeepWell™ plates were all purchased from Sigma Aldrich.

- 1.  _Characterization of MNPs_

Characterization of iron oxide (Fe3O4) magnetic nanoparticles was conducted using different techniques. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed using a TGA Q50 instrument (TA Instruments). The experiment was conducted under a nitrogen gas flow rate of 60 mL/

min. The temperature ramp spanned from 25 ◦C to 950 ◦C, with a

heating rate of 10 ◦C/min. TEM micrographs were captured using a Philips–FEI, Morgagni-268 transmission electron microscope (Hillsboro, USA) operating at an acceleration voltage of 80 kV. The surface ζ-po-tential and hydrodynamic size of CD-modified MNPs were assessed using a Zetasizer Nano ZS instrument (Malvern Instruments, UK). The samples were prepared following protocols as described previously ([Yallapu et al., 2011](#_bookmark55)). Prior to each measurement, particle suspensions at a concentration of 8 μg/mL in Milli-Q water were sonicated for 30 s and immediately subjected to ζ-potential and DLS analysis.

- 1.  _Model toxin solution_

Solid chemicals were carefully weighed using a high-precision elec-tronic balance (XPE105, Mettler Toledo, Switzerland, d = 0.01 mg). A concentrated solution of each chemical was prepared using LC-MS grade water. To prepare the concentrated solution of uremic toxins, a specific volume of each stock solution was mixed, and uric acid in powder form

was added last. The volume was then adjusted to 100 mL using LC-MS grade water. Next, 100 mL of 20 mM PBS was added to create a model uremic toxin solution in 10 mM PBS with a pH of 7.4. Finally, the

solution was divided into aliquots and stored at —80 ◦C until use.

- 1.  _Synthesis of CD-modified MNPs_

CD-modified MNPs were synthesized using a co-precipitation method based on established protocols ([Monteiro et al., 2017](#_bookmark36); [Yallapu](#_bookmark55) [et al., 2011](#_bookmark55)). Milli-Q water was degassed for 1 h and subsequently purged with ultrapure nitrogen gas for 20 min. In a three-necked and

round-bottom glass flask equipped with a nitrogen inlet, a 25 mL solu-tion containing Fe3+ and Fe2+ ions in a molar ratio of 2:1, along with 100 μg of CD, was added. The mixture was then stirred at 400 rpm for 20

min. Next, approximately 1.5 mL of ammonium hydroxide solution was added dropwise at a constant rate while stirring at 900 rpm. The resulting suspension of nanoparticles was stirred gently overnight to allow excess ammonia to evaporate. The nanoparticle precipitates were washed with Milli-Q water multiple times. Subsequently, the suspension of nanoparticles was stirred with a solution of sodium citrate (500 mg/ mL) overnight. The resulting product was rewashed with Milli-Q water,

and the suspension of nanoparticles in water was stored at 4 ◦C for

subsequent characterization.

- 1.  _Toxin adsorption_

Before the experiments, all tubes were rinsed with LC-MS grade methanol and dried. In each adsorption experiment, 0.25 mg of nano-particles were incubated with 0.5 mL of uremic toxin solution for 1 and 4 h at 37 ◦C. Upon incubation, the MNPs were collected on the side of the tube using a magnet, and the supernatant was carefully removed. To

prevent any false readings caused by the trapped solution, the pellet of nanoparticles underwent a gentle flow of nitrogen gas to remove any remaining excess solution. The nanoparticles were resuspended in 100 μL of LC-MS grade methanol and incubated for 24 h at 37 ◦C to ensure complete desorption of uremic toxins.

- 1.  _LC-MS quantification_

A quantitative metabolomics approach utilizing reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) tandem mass spectroscopy was employed to analyze the eluted uremic toxins ([Li, Sharaf, Zhang,](#_bookmark31) [et al., 2023](#_bookmark31); [Zhang et al., 2020](#_bookmark56)). The analysis used an Agilent 1290 series UHPLC system and an Agilent reversed-phase Zorbax Eclipse XDB C18 column (3.0 mm × 100 mm, 3.5 μm particle size, 80 Å pore size). Online

LC-MS/MS was performed using an AB SCIEX QTRAP® 5500 mass

spectrometer, with Analyst® 1.6.3 as the controlling software. Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mode was employed, applying positive/ negative electrospray ionization. The metabolomics raw data was pro-cessed using Multi Quant™ 3.0.3.

- 1.  _Statistical analysis_

To evaluate the significance of differences between various results, the statistical analysis was conducted using an unpaired _t_\-test, with a p-value threshold of 0.05. One-way ANOVA was used for comparisons involving more than two groups.

## Results and discussion

- 1.  _Molecular characterization of MNPs_
        1. _Size characterization via DLS and TEM_

Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) tend to cluster in an aqueous solu-tion due to their size, surface charge, morphology, and magnetic prop-erties ([Dabaghi & Hilger, 2020](#_bookmark16)). DLS analyses for bare iron oxide nanoparticles have shown cluster sizes ranging from ~200 to ~340 nm ([Table 2](#_bookmark4)) ([Monteiro et al., 2017](#_bookmark36); [Yallapu et al., 2011](#_bookmark55)). Respective cluster size and polydispersity index (PI) values of 301.4, 94, 100, 95 nm and

0.65, 0.16, 0.17, 0.26 for bare, α-, β-, and γ-MNPs were obtained ([Table 2](#_bookmark4)). Particles coated with CDs (α, β, or γ) had a more uniform size distribution and smaller overall cluster size compared to bare MNPs; consistent with previous observations and attributed to the presence of CDs during the reduction of iron ions (Fe2+ and Fe3+) ([Yallapu et al.,](#_bookmark55) [2011](#_bookmark55)), while citrate ions stabilize the coating and enhance their

dispersion stability and protect against oxidation ([Monteiro et al.,](#_bookmark36)

[2017](#_bookmark36)). TEM micrographs confirmed that CD modification affected MNP cluster size ([Table 2](#_bookmark4), [Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)A). Even though drying may affect the cluster properties, the differences between bare and modified surfaces were significant: bare particles exhibited extensive clustering, forming large clumps, whereas CD-coated particles formed smaller, more compact groups ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)A). This change in size may arise from the hydroxyl groups present in CDs acting as chelating agents for growing iron oxides and impede the continued growth of nanoparticles through steric hindrance ([Monteiro et al., 2017](#_bookmark36); [Sun et al., 2008](#_bookmark43)). It should also be noted that if

nanoparticles form aggregates or clusters, DLS will measure the hydro-dynamic size of that cluster. However, TEM micrographs provide a direct visual representation of the nanoparticles, enabling the visuali-zation of individual particles and their arrangements. TEM data showed that particle sizes decreased upon CD coating with particle diameters of 7–15 nm for bare MNPs and 5–12 nm for CD-coated ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)B). Previous studies have indicated that MNPs, synthesized initially _via_ the co-precipitation method and subsequently subjected to covalent grafting with carboxymethyl-β-cyclodextrin, exhibited no notable disparity in

grain size pre- and post-coating ([Agotegaray et al., 2020](#_bookmark12)). This high-lights the impact of CDs in the co-precipitation process, leading to a slightly diminished grain size, as evidenced by TEM micrographs. The size distribution of MNP clusters measured using DLS is shown in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)C.

- -   1.  _Surface charge characterization_

ζ-potential measurements revealed distinct differences upon CD modification of the MNPs. Bare MNPs exhibited a ζ-potential of +5 ±

0.2 mV ([Table 2](#_bookmark4)), whereas α-, β-, and γ-MNP particles were —23.3 ± 0.6,

—21.2 ± 0.4, and —23.5 ± 0.4 mV. Showing that CD-coated particles

dramatically shifted to negative ζ-potential values, which has been correlated with improved suspension stability ([Choi, Lee, Song, & Sohn,](#_bookmark14) [2015](#_bookmark14)). Previous studies have demonstrated a notable alteration in ζ-potential values, shifting from +6.17 for uncoated MNPs to negative

values ranging from approximately —18 to —32, depending on the initial

concentration of β-CD upon coating ([Yallapu et al., 2011](#_bookmark55)).

- -   1.  _Film hydration and weight loss_

The effect of CD film composition on the resulting film hydration and the overall amount of CD present in the film was determined using TGA. Weight loss below 100 ◦C has been attributed to the evaporation of bulk water trapped within the particle matrix ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark6)). Subsequent weight loss between 100 ◦C and 200 ◦C corresponds with the loss of adsorbed vicinal water molecules, whereas 200–390C represents the breaking of C–O and C–C bonds ([Li, Sharaf, Zhang, et al., 2023](#_bookmark31)). At this point, a residue forms, which undergoes further decomposition at a slower rate for temperatures exceeding 400 ◦C ([Trotta, Zanetti, & Camino, 2000](#_bookmark46)). Bare MNPs showed the lowest weight loss for both bulk and vicinal water content compared to all CD-modified MNPs, likely due to the hydration of CDs ([Shikata, Takahashi, & Satokawa, 2007](#_bookmark42)). Atomistic molecular dynamics simulations have confirmed that the total average number of hydrogen bonds per CD molecule increases from 32.7 to 43.0 for α- and γ-CD, respectively ([Sandilya, Natarajan, & Priya, 2020](#_bookmark40)). The α-, β-, and γ-CDs differ in the number of glucose units (α-CD: n = 6, β-CD: n = 7,

γ-CD: n = 8) and, consequently, in the availability of OH groups for

hydrogen bonding. This could explain the differences observed in vicinal water levels among α-, β-, and γ-MNPs ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark6)).

Total weight loss for bare, α-, β-, and γ-MNPs were found to be 3.8, 7.2, 7.5, and 11.7 wt%, respectively. The fractional weight loss associ-ated with α-, β-, γ-CD + citrate content was 3.4, 3.7, and 7.9 wt%, respectively. The weight loss observed in the CD-coated MNPs

corresponds to the decomposition of the functional groups present on CD, which confirms the integration of CD layers onto the surfaces of the MNPs. Moreover, given that there is only one glucose subunit difference between β-, and γ-MNPs, the significant difference in weight loss starting at 200 ◦C between these systems may indicate that more γ-MNPs are

present in the film. This was also different than previous TGA results

showing a consistent thermal degradation profile across various types of CDs, where 70–80 % weight loss occurred between 250 and 400 ◦C. There have not been any studies directly comparing the thermal degradation patterns of MNPs coated with α-, β-, and γ-CDs. However, in previous studies where β-MNPs were synthesized using a comparable

concentration of β-CD, bare particles exhibited a total weight loss of approximately 6.78 wt%, while β-MNPs showed a fractional weight loss of 4.6 wt% ([Yallapu et al., 2011](#_bookmark55)). Another study demonstrated a total weight loss of 10.6 wt% for bare MNPs, with a fractional weight loss of

4.9 wt% associated with β-CD + citrate content ([Monteiro et al., 2017](#_bookmark36)).

- 1.  _Effect of CD coating on uremic toxin adsorption_

The adsorption of uremic toxins as a function of MNPs surface chemistry and incubation time (1 or 4 h) in a model solution ([Table 1](#_bookmark3)) containing multiple toxins was evaluated using quantitative LC-MS. This approach was used to quantify adsorbed uremic toxins, which provided insight into their binding capacity, adsorption specificity, and adsorbed stability over time. It was observed that dimethylarginine, kynurenine,

methylhistidine, quinolinic acid, spermidine, spermine, and xanthine were below the level of detection (<LOD). Nevertheless, all particles adsorbed toxins when incubated in this complex solution ([Table 3](#_bookmark7), [Fig. 3](#_bookmark8)).

The total adsorbed amount of uremic toxins ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark8)) was largely affected by pyruvic acid due to its substantial adsorption across all MNP systems ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)). Bound uremic toxins were compared, and those with statistical differences were identified (_p_ < 0.05, unpaired _t_\-test, [Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)). Compared to bare MNPs, there were statistically higher adsorption

levels for creatinine, phenylalanine, and trimethylamine N-oxide for α-, β-, and γ-MNPs at both the 1 and 4-hr adsorption time points ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)A-C). Surprisingly, pyruvic acid exhibited significantly higher adsorption to bare MNP in a 4-hr incubation period than α-, β-, and γ-CD MNPs under the same incubation conditions ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)D). Given that many toxins showed no significant difference in adsorption levels between the 1 and 4-hr intervals, it may be that up to a 1-hr incubation is needed to achieve maximal adsorption capacity. This was not observed for other systems, where the total adsorbed amount did not stabilize within 1-hr of incu-bation ([Li, Sharaf, Zhang, et al., 2023](#_bookmark31)).

Adsorption specificity was evaluated by comparing the adsorbed uremic toxin profile with the initial solution ([Table 4](#_bookmark10)). Pyruvic acid had the highest binding ratio, reaching a 14 to 25-fold increase over its initial solution fraction. This becomes even more notable when considering the pyruvic acid’s initial solution mol% was only 3.2 % of the total, suggesting a substantial affinity with all MNP systems. Whereas creatinine and hippuric acid had a very high amount within the initial solution (_i.e._, ~30 mol%), which was not altered upon adsorption; concentration effects did not solely drive adsorption levels. This was previously observed for uremic toxin adsorption to poly(2-(meth-acryloyloxy)ethyl phosphorylcholine-_co_\-β-CD) MNPs, supporting the fact that adsorption is not driven only by solution concentration ([Li,](#_bookmark31) [Sharaf, Zhang, et al., 2023](#_bookmark31)).

While other compounds did not exhibit a mol% increase comparable

to pyruvic acid, most displayed an upward trend in preferential adsorption upon CD coating, in contrast to bare MNPs. This trend aligned with observations of higher surface area and increased carbo-hydrate content in CD-coated particles, as confirmed by DLS, TEM, and TGA analysis. This is even more evident considering bare MNP surfaces did not yield a binding capacity reaching 10 % of the initial mol fraction for most compounds (dark blue, [Table 4](#_bookmark10)). compared to bare iron oxides, it has been shown that poly-β-CDs are more effective in the absorption of certain toxins such as p-cresol surface compared to zirconium-based metal–organic frameworks (NU-1000) ([Kato et al., 2019](#_bookmark24); [Li et al., 2020](#_bookmark29)).

The effect of incubation time on uremic toxin adsorption was used to understand the stability of adsorbed toxins over 4 h ([Table 5](#_bookmark11)). When interpreting [Table 5](#_bookmark11), it is important to consider the influence that the high amounts of adsorbed pyruvic acid have ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)D). CD-coated MNPs demonstrated a notable upward trend in the mol% of adsorbed toxins as

the incubation time increased from 1 to 4 h, except for pyruvic acid ([Table 5](#_bookmark11)). Likely, the displacement of the large pyruvic acid allowed for more moles of other toxins to be adsorbed. γ-MNPs exhibited the highest increase in mol% with only a major decrease for uridine in this time-frame. The increased adsorption trend in γ-MNPs aligns with a higher surface area of γ-MNPs compared to bare types, and larger cavity size within γ-CD structure, which may facilitate enhanced toxin adsorption. α-CD films exhibited an increasing trend in mol% with increasing adsorption time for all compounds except pyruvic acid. While not reaching the same levels observed in γ- and α-CD films, β-CD films also exhibited a general increase in mol% over time for most compounds. While the mol% of 3-deoxyglucosone remained unchanged in β-MNPs, a substantial increase in mol% from 1 to 4 h of adsorption time was observed in α- and γ-MNPs. Phenylalanine showed a substantial increase in mol% for all types of CD-MNPs compared to bare MNPs. Previous studies have shown that the hydrophobic side chain of aromatic amino acids can directly penetrate the cavities of CDs ([Rudolph, Riedel, &](#_bookmark38) [Henle, 2018](#_bookmark38)). Thus, the aromatic benzene ring within the structure of phenylalanine likely serves as the primary contributor to the hydro-phobic effect between this amino acid and the CD films. Compared to other MNPs, γ-MNPs showed a substantial increase in mol% of 3-indole-acetic acid with increasing adsorption time. This suggests that the chemical structure of 3-indoleacetic acid, with its indole ring, promotes hydrophobic interactions, while its carboxylate group might enhance electrostatic interactions. The γ-MNPs also exhibited a noticeable in-crease in mol% for guanidinopropionic acid, orotic acid, hippuric acid, and p-cresol sulfate. This aligns with more accessible interactive groups on γ-CD-coated surfaces compared to the other MNP types. β-CD-modified surfaces have been previously used in designing electrodes for selective detection of uric acid in solution ([Zheng, Wu, Lin, Nie, & Rui,](#_bookmark58) [2001](#_bookmark58)). In this study, a comparable mol% increase was observed for bare and β-MNPs with increasing adsorption time, however a substantial increase in mol% upon increasing adsorption time was observed in α-CD films, which reached highest in γ-CD films. ## Conclusions

Magnetic nanoparticles were synthesized _via_ co-precipitation of ferric chlorides in the presence of different types of CDs (α, β, and γ). Various analytical techniques, including TGA, TEM, DLS, and ζ-poten-tial, were employed to investigate the chemical and physical properties of these particles. TGA analysis demonstrated the chemical composition and weight loss patterns of each system, where CD-MNPs exhibited a fractional weight loss of 3.4 %, 3.7 %, and 7.9 % for α-, β-, and γ-CD +

citrate content, respectively. DLS and TEM analyses indicated that CD-

coated particles displayed a more uniform size distribution and smaller overall cluster and grain sizes compared to bare MNPs. The CD coating led to a notable shift towards negative ζ-potential values, a modification linked with improved suspension stability, proving more suitable for biomedical applications.

To investigate the adsorption dynamics of uremic toxins, a freshly prepared solution containing selected uremic toxins ([Table 1](#_bookmark3)), reflecting typical concentrations observed in individuals with kidney dysfunction, was incubated with synthesized nano-adsorbents. The adsorption was quantified using LC-MS/MS, revealing that for a broad range of toxins, the maximal adsorption capacity was achieved by all CD-MNPs within 1 h of incubation time. Pyruvic acid exhibited the highest adsorption profile by all MNP systems. α-, β-, and γ-MNPs demonstrated signifi-cantly higher adsorption levels for creatinine, phenylalanine, and tri-methylamine N-oxide compared to bare MNPs at both adsorption time points. The modification with CD was observed to enhance the adsorp-tion stability of toxins, with γ-CD films demonstrating maximal stability across various toxins.

To summarize, we have successfully synthesized MNPs coated with various CDs and assessed their applicability as adsorbents for blood clearance. While prior research focused on using CDs to adsorb indi-vidual toxins or a combination of a few uremic toxins to enhance blood clearance, our study pioneers the evaluation of magnetite nanoparticles coated with diverse CD variants for their efficacy in adsorbing a broad spectrum of uremic toxins. Our findings indicate that the hypothesis was correct in that these physisorbed coating of CDs on MNPs have the po-tential to specifically bind different types of uremic toxins in a manner unrelated to solution concentration, where this binding for some toxins is dynamic, while others remain bound in a stable manner.
